title: Algorithms & Data Structures II: Trees, Heaps, Hashing, and Graphs
description: The second half of a first course: recursion and the call stack, hash tables, binary and binary-search trees, depth-first and breadth-first traversal, binary heaps, and graph search including shortest paths — in TypeScript, with execution traces and debugging exercises.

infoObjects.title: Choosing the Right Structure
infoObjects.content:
Part 2 covered four structures and two traversal orders. The useful skill now is not recalling any one of them, but knowing which to reach for.

| Structure | Lookup | Ordered? | Reach for it when |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hash table | O(1) average | no | you need membership or key to value, and never order |
| Binary search tree | O(log n) balanced, O(n) degenerate | fully sorted | you need lookup *and* in-order iteration |
| Binary heap | O(1) peek min, O(log n) push | partially | you only ever need the smallest (or largest) item |
| Adjacency list | O(degree) per vertex | no | edges are sparse relative to vertices |

The heap is the one people over-reach for: it does **not** support "find an arbitrary value" any faster than a plain array, because siblings are unordered. It only makes the extreme cheap.

And for traversals: **BFS** for shortest paths and anything level-related, **DFS** for exhaustive exploration, cycle detection, and topological work. DFS also costs stack depth proportional to the longest path, which on a deep graph can overflow where BFS's explicit queue would not.
